templates.title: Metered tokens versus billed tokens

sections.scenario: An API platform meters every model request in tokens: prompt tokens in, completion tokens out. A nightly billing job writes one total per project per UTC day. Finance has found days where the billed total and the metered total disagree, and asks for a daily report of the project-days that drift by more than {{threshold}} tokens.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns usage_date, project_id, metered_tokens, billed_tokens, diff (where diff = billed_tokens - metered_tokens) for every project-day where |diff| > {{threshold}}, ordered by usage_date, project_id. Metered tokens are prompt_tokens + completion_tokens over requests with status = 'ok', attributed to the UTC date of event_ts. {{retries}} {{gaps}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Strictly greater than {{threshold}}: a drift of exactly {{threshold}} is not reported. The sample has {{events}} usage rows; production has billions per day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema and volumes. event_ts is when the request was served; ingested_at is when the usage record reached the warehouse.
sections.criteria: Deduplicates before aggregating; attributes by event time; ok-only; full outer join with zero-fill; strict threshold; deterministic ordering; can explain how to make the report final under late data.

clarifications.q: Which date does a request belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC date of event_ts, not of ingested_at.

clarifications.q: Do errored requests count?
clarifications.a: No. Only status = 'ok' is billable.

clarifications.q: What if the same request appears twice?
clarifications.a: Keep one row per request_id: the copy with the latest ingested_at.

clarifications.q: What if a project-day exists only in billing, or only in usage?
clarifications.a: Report it if the drift exceeds the threshold, treating the missing side as 0.

clarifications.q: Is the threshold inclusive?
clarifications.a: No. Report only when the absolute difference is strictly greater.

hints: Build the metered side first, in its own CTE, at the same grain as billing: one row per (usage_date, project_id).
Deduplicate before you aggregate. DISTINCT ON (request_id) … ORDER BY request_id, ingested_at DESC is one way.
A row that exists on only one side survives a FULL OUTER JOIN; use COALESCE on both keys and both totals.
followups: Billing runs at 02:00 UTC, but usage can arrive up to 6 hours late. How do you make the report final, and how do you correct a day that was already billed?
At billions of rows a day, which physical design makes this query cheap: partitioning, clustering, or a pre-aggregated daily metered table? What keeps that table correct when late events land?
Some drift is legitimate: credits, free-tier allowances and batch discounts. How do you model them so reconciliation compares like with like?
Write the data-quality check you would run before finance sees the report, and say what it does when it fails.

rules.ask: What happens to a project that was billed but sent no usage that day, and to one that used tokens but has no billing line?
Your deduplication keeps one row per request_id. What if two copies share the same ingested_at?
Which timestamp decides the billing day, and what goes wrong if you pick the other one near midnight?
How would you prove to finance that every metered token is counted exactly once?

templates.title: Hourly p95 latency regressions by model family

sections.scenario: An inference API serves several model families. The on-call dashboard shows, for every family and every hour, the traffic, the error rate and the p95 latency of successful requests, and it flags an hour whose p95 rose more than {{pct}}% over the hour before. You are writing the query behind that panel for the report window {{start}} to {{end}}.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns hour_start, model_family, requests, error_rate, p95_ms, prev_p95_ms, regressed: one row for every family in model_families and every hour from {{start}} to {{end}} inclusive ({{hours}} hours), ordered by hour_start, model_family. An event belongs to the UTC hour date_trunc('hour', event_ts). requests counts every request in the hour; error_rate is the share whose status is not 'ok' (NULL when there were no requests). p95_ms is percentile_cont(0.95) of latency_ms over status = 'ok' requests only (NULL when there were none). prev_p95_ms is the same family's p95_ms for the immediately preceding clock hour. regressed is true when both are present and p95_ms > prev_p95_ms * (1 + {{pct}} / 100.0), otherwise false. {{gaps}} {{baseline}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The threshold is strict: a rise of exactly {{pct}}% is not a regression. regressed is never NULL. The sample has {{events}} events; assume billions per day in production.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical families, latencies and volumes. latency_ms is the server-side duration of a request; for a timeout it is the timeout limit, not a serving time.
sections.criteria: p95 over successful requests with percentile_cont; error_rate over all requests; a complete hour grid; LAG over the grid so "previous" means the previous clock hour, including the baseline before the window; strict, NULL-safe regressed; deterministic order; can explain why percentiles are not additive and how to alert robustly.

clarifications.q: Do failed requests count in the p95?
clarifications.a: No. The p95 is over status = 'ok' only. Failed requests count in requests and error_rate.

clarifications.q: Which statuses are failures?
clarifications.a: Every status other than 'ok': here 'error' and 'timeout'.

clarifications.q: Which percentile?
clarifications.a: percentile_cont, which interpolates linearly between the two values either side of the 95th percentile. Not percentile_disc.

clarifications.q: What is "the previous hour" if the family had no traffic then?
clarifications.a: It is always the immediately preceding clock hour. If that hour has no p95, there is nothing to compare with and the row is not a regression.

clarifications.q: Where does an event at exactly 10:00:00 belong?
clarifications.a: To the 10:00 hour.

clarifications.q: Is a rise of exactly {{pct}}% a regression?
clarifications.a: No. Only strictly more.

hints: Aggregate per (hour, family) first: COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status <> 'ok'), and percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) FILTER (WHERE status = 'ok').
LAG means "previous hour" only if every hour has a row. Build the grid with generate_series(...) × model_families, LEFT JOIN the hourly stats onto it, then apply LAG.
Restrict to the report window after LAG has run, not before.
followups: The panel now needs p99 as well, broken down by region. What changes in the query, and why does an exact percentile get expensive at billions of rows per hour?
Raw latencies are kept for 7 days. How do you store hourly latency so that a daily or weekly p95 can still be computed later, and why is the average of 24 hourly p95s not the daily p95?
One hour with six requests fires an alert. How would you make the regression rule robust without hiding real regressions?
The panel must refresh every minute while events arrive up to 10 minutes late. How do you compute it incrementally, and when is an hour final?

rules.ask: percentile_disc and percentile_cont differ most on small samples. Which would you alert on, and what does each return for 12 requests?
Can you average hourly p95s to get a daily p95? If not, what would you store instead so the daily figure stays exact or bounded?
What does your LAG return for the hour right after an hour with no traffic, and how do you know the row it read is the previous clock hour?
If failed requests are removed in WHERE, what happens to error_rate, and to an hour in which every request failed?
The grid is families × hours. How does that scale to 500 families in per-minute buckets over 30 days, and what would you do instead?

templates.title: First context-window overflow per conversation session
templates.subtopic: gaps and islands, running sums, window frames

sections.scenario: A chat product sends the whole session history back to the model on every turn, so the context grows turn by turn. After a spell of inactivity the client starts a fresh session with an empty history. Before tuning truncation and summarisation, the team wants to know where sessions first outgrow their model's context window.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns, for every session whose context ever exceeds its model's window, the first message where it does: conversation_id, session_no, turn_no, message_id, context_tokens, context_window, ordered by conversation_id, session_no. Within a conversation, messages are ordered by sent_at, message_id. A conversation's first message starts session 1; a message that arrives more than {{gap}} minutes after the previous message of the same conversation starts the next session. turn_no is the message's 1-based position in its session. context_tokens is the conversation's system_tokens plus the running total of tokens over the session's messages up to and including this one. context_window comes from the conversation's model. {{models_rule}} {{ties_rule}} {{system_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A gap of exactly {{gap}} minutes continues the session. A context exactly equal to the window still fits: report only context_tokens > context_window. One row per overflowing session. The sample has {{messages}} messages.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical models and context windows; they are not any real model's limits. tokens is the message's metered token count. A real client would also reserve room for the reply being generated; this exercise ignores that.
sections.criteria: Correct sessionisation per conversation with a strict gap; deterministic order with the message_id tie-break; an explicit ROWS frame; totals reset per session and start from the system prompt; strict overflow test; one row per overflowing session; can discuss a truncation policy and incremental sessionisation.

clarifications.q: Does a gap of exactly {{gap}} minutes start a new session?
clarifications.a: No. Only a gap of strictly more than {{gap}} minutes does.

clarifications.q: What if two messages in a conversation have the same sent_at?
clarifications.a: The lower message_id came first. Your ordering must be fully deterministic.

clarifications.q: Does a context equal to the window overflow?
clarifications.a: No. Strictly greater only.

clarifications.q: Does a new session carry tokens over from the previous one?
clarifications.a: No. Every session starts from system_tokens alone.

clarifications.q: Should I report every message after the overflow?
clarifications.a: No. Only the first overflowing message of each session; sessions that never overflow are not reported.

hints: This is gaps and islands: LAG(sent_at) per conversation, a 1 where the gap is more than the limit (or there is no previous message), and a running SUM of those flags is session_no.

The running total needs an explicit frame: SUM(tokens) OVER (PARTITION BY conversation_id, session_no ORDER BY sent_at, message_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). The default frame is RANGE, which treats rows with equal ORDER BY values as one.
Filter to overflowing rows, then keep the first per session with DISTINCT ON or ROW_NUMBER().
followups: Product changes the policy: instead of a new session, the client drops the oldest messages until the context fits. Describe how you would compute the context at every turn now, and why a single running sum no longer expresses it.
At billions of messages, how do you assign session_no incrementally as messages arrive, and what happens when a late message lands inside a gap and joins two sessions into one?
Report the median and p90 number of turns before overflow, per model. What bias do you introduce by looking only at sessions that overflowed, and how would you correct for it?
A conversation switches model mid-session, and the two models count tokens differently. How do you change the schema and the query?

rules.ask: Two messages share a sent_at. What does your running SUM return for the first of them, and why?
Why ROWS rather than RANGE here? Construct the input on which they differ.
A late message arrives in the middle of a three-hour gap and closes it. Which session numbers change, and how would an incremental pipeline repair them?
A session reaches exactly the window. Does it overflow? Point to the line of your query that decides it.
How do you guarantee the "first" overflowing message is unique when timestamps tie?

templates.title: Sliding-window token rate limiter

sections.scenario: An API gateway enforces usage limits per project over a sliding 60-second window. Limits are measured in tokens per minute (TPM) and, for some plans, requests per minute (RPM), the same two dimensions public model APIs document. You are writing the admission decision for a replay of the gateway log.
sections.problem: Implement admit(requests, tpm, rpm=None). requests is a list of (ts_ms, project_id, tokens) sorted by ts_ms. Return one boolean per request. A request is admitted when the tokens of the project's admitted requests in the window (ts_ms − 60000, ts_ms], plus its own tokens, stay within tpm[project_id]. {{limit_rule}} {{rpm_rule}} A rejected request consumes nothing.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 requests; 1 ≤ tokens ≤ 10⁶; timestamps are non-decreasing integers. Amortised O(1) work per request is expected.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical limits and traffic. The window is half-open: a request exactly 60 000 ms older has left it.
sections.criteria: Correct half-open window; rejected requests do not consume; per-project state; amortised O(1) with a justification; handles unknown projects and simultaneous timestamps; discusses distributed enforcement honestly.

clarifications.q: Is the window inclusive of a request exactly 60 seconds older?
clarifications.a: No. The window is (ts − 60000, ts]; a request exactly 60 000 ms older has left it.

clarifications.q: Do rejected requests count toward the limit?
clarifications.a: No. Only admitted requests consume capacity.

clarifications.q: What about a project with no configured limit?
clarifications.a: Reject it.

clarifications.q: Can several requests share a timestamp?
clarifications.a: Yes. Process them in list order.

hints: Keep, per project, a queue of the admitted requests still inside the window and a running token total.
Before deciding on a request, drop from the front of that project's queue everything at or before ts − 60000.
Each request is pushed once and popped at most once, which is where amortised O(1) comes from.
followups: The gateway now runs on 40 machines. How do you enforce one project-wide limit without a central lock on every request?
A fixed-window counter is much cheaper than a sliding log. What does it get wrong at window boundaries, and how much over the limit can a client get?
Tokens are only known after the response is generated. How do you admit a request before you know its true cost, and how do you reconcile afterwards?
Memory is per project per window. What happens with 2 million active projects, and how would you bound it?

rules.ask: Every request now makes a network round trip to that store. What is your p99 overhead, and what does the gateway do when the store is slow or down?
Show a request pattern that exceeds the limit by nearly 2× under your fixed window.
How does a token bucket's behaviour differ from the sliding window this question specifies, and when is that difference acceptable?
What is the time complexity per request when 10 000 requests sit in the window?

templates.title: Global p95 per window from regional latency streams
templates.subtopic: k-way merge of sorted streams, order statistics

sections.scenario: Each serving region of an inference API writes its own request log, sorted by time. The observability service builds a global latency view by merging those regional streams and reporting the p95 per time window. The streams are long-lived: a report on a few minutes must not read a day of data.
sections.problem: Implement window_p95(logs, t0, width, n_windows, step=None, min_count=1). logs holds K iterables, one per region, each yielding (ts_ms, latency_ms) sorted by ts_ms. Return a list of n_windows values: for each window, the nearest-rank p95 of the latencies of every region's events in it: sort them ascending and take the value at 1-based rank ⌈0.95·n⌉. {{window_rule}} {{count_rule}} Read the logs lazily: a log can be far longer than the report period, so consume each one only as far as the report needs.
sections.constraints: Up to 64 regions and 2 000 000 events per log, of which the report period covers a small fraction. Merging the M events the report needs should cost O(M log K); memory O(K + M).
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical regions, rates and latencies. Region clocks are treated as synchronised. Events before t0 or at or after the end of the last window are ignored.
sections.criteria: Lazy k-way merge with a heap and a correct stop condition; half-open windows; nearest-rank arithmetic in integers; empty windows and min_count; correct window assignment for hopping windows; a clear complexity argument; a credible discussion of watermarks and mergeable sketches.

clarifications.q: Are window boundaries inclusive?
clarifications.a: A window is [start, start + width): the start is in, the end is out.

clarifications.q: Which p95 definition?
clarifications.a: Nearest rank: the ⌈0.95·n⌉-th smallest value, a latency that actually occurred. No interpolation. For n = 20 that is the 19th value.

clarifications.q: Two regions have an event at the same timestamp.
clarifications.a: Both count. Their relative order does not matter.

clarifications.q: Can I call list() on a log?
clarifications.a: On the samples, yes. The timing test passes streams about 80 times longer than the report, so reading them to the end will not finish in time.

clarifications.q: Can a window be empty?
clarifications.a: Yes. It reports None.

hints: Keep a min-heap holding the next event of each region. Pop the smallest, then push that region's next event: that is the global time order, one event at a time.
Every log is sorted, so once the smallest timestamp in the heap is at or past the end of the last window, nothing that is left can fall inside it. Stop there.
Map each event to its window(s) arithmetically and collect latencies per window in a dict or list; select the rank-th value per window at the end.
followups: One region's collector runs 30 seconds behind. When can you safely emit window i, and what do you do with an event that arrives after you have emitted its window?
Per-window memory is O(events). Replace the exact p95 with a mergeable sketch. What error guarantee do you get, and why can per-region sketches be merged when per-region p95 values cannot?
K becomes 5 000 streams (one per host). What does each event cost now, and when would batching or a different structure beat a binary heap?
The panel wants a p95 over the last 60 seconds, updated on every event. Design it with two heaps and lazy deletion, and give its complexity.

rules.ask: Your solution reads every log to the end. What happens when each log is an unbounded live stream?
heapq.merge is lazy. Where does your loop stop reading, and what does each event cost?
Can you combine per-region p95 values into a global p95? Give a counterexample.
This spec uses nearest rank. When would you prefer interpolation, and what does each give for 20 samples?

templates.title: Cost-optimal micro-batching for an inference server

sections.scenario: An inference server groups queued requests into batches before running them on a GPU. Every request in a batch is padded to the longest sequence in that batch, so one long prompt makes the whole batch expensive, and every batch also pays a fixed launch overhead. The scheduler has a queue of requests and wants to know the cheapest way to batch all of them.
sections.problem: Implement min_batch_cost(lengths, max_batch, overhead, token_budget=None, shapes=None). lengths holds the sequence length of each queued request, in arrival order. Split the requests into batches of at most max_batch requests; any request may go in any batch. A batch of k requests whose longest sequence is m costs m × k + overhead. {{budget_rule}} {{shape_rule}} Return the minimum total cost of running every request exactly once.
sections.constraints: 0 ≤ len(lengths) ≤ 10 000; 1 ≤ length ≤ 4096; 1 ≤ max_batch ≤ 128; 0 ≤ overhead ≤ 10⁶. Every single request is runnable on its own. An O(n log n + n·B) solution, where B is max_batch, is expected.
sections.assumptions: The cost model is a hypothetical simplification: real attention cost is not linear in length, and real engines batch continuously. Lengths and overheads are invented. An empty queue costs 0.
sections.criteria: Sorts and justifies contiguity with an exchange argument; correct DP base case and transitions; uses the sorted order to get each batch's maximum in O(1); handles the budget (inclusive) and padded shapes; O(n log n + n·B) time and O(n) space; empty queue and single request handled; can discuss reconstruction and online batching.

clarifications.q: Do batches have to follow arrival order?
clarifications.a: No. Any request may go in any batch; only the total cost matters.

clarifications.q: Is the cost per batch the sum of lengths or the padded size?
clarifications.a: The padded size: the longest length in the batch times the number of slots it occupies.

clarifications.q: Can a batch be empty, or can a request run twice?
clarifications.a: No. Every request runs exactly once, and a batch has at least one request.

clarifications.q: Do I need to return the batches themselves?
clarifications.a: Return only the cost. Being able to reconstruct the batches is a follow-up.

clarifications.q: Is the budget check inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A batch whose padded tokens equal token_budget is allowed.

hints: Sort the lengths. Argue that some optimal answer only ever groups requests that are adjacent in sorted order.

Exchange argument: if a batch with maximum m holds a short request while a longer one (still ≤ m) sits in another batch, swapping them never raises either batch's maximum and keeps every batch size the same.
Let dp[i] be the cheapest cost for the i shortest requests. The last batch is sorted[j:i], and its maximum is simply sorted[i-1].
If padded size never shrinks as k grows, once one k breaks the budget every larger k does too, so you can stop the inner loop early.
followups: Return the batches as well as the cost. What do you store, and how do you choose among equally cheap batchings?
max_batch grows to the size of the queue (10 000). The O(n·B) recurrence becomes quadratic. How can you speed it up? (The cost term sorted[i-1] × (i − j) is linear in j.)
Requests keep arriving, and each one has a latency deadline. How does the offline optimum change when you must decide now without knowing the rest of the queue?
Real attention cost grows faster than linearly with sequence length. Which parts of your argument still hold if the batch cost is f(m) × k for any increasing f?

rules.ask: Give a small input where filling every batch to max_batch is not optimal, and say what your greedy misses.
How many partitions does a queue of 30 requests have, and what property lets you avoid enumerating them?
After sorting, what is the maximum of sorted[j:i]? What does recomputing it cost you overall?
With 10 000 queued requests, what happens to Python's recursion depth, and how would you write it bottom-up?
The batch size is capped at B, so old lines expire. How does your structure remove them, and why is that still amortised O(1)?

templates.title: Staged model rollout — earliest finish time
templates.subtopic: topological sort, longest path in a DAG, cycle detection

sections.scenario: A new model version is rolled out in stages: weights are uploaded, evaluations gate the release, serving shards are updated, traffic is ramped and dashboards are switched. Some steps depend on others and the rest run in parallel. The release manager wants the earliest time the whole rollout can finish, and needs the plan rejected if someone has introduced a circular dependency.
sections.problem: Implement rollout_finish(durations, deps, with_path=False). durations maps each step to its duration in minutes. {{dep_rule}} A step with no dependencies starts at minute 0, and every step starts as early as its dependencies allow; any number of steps can run at once. {{return_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 50 000 steps and 200 000 dependencies. Durations and soak times are non-negative integers. Chains can be tens of thousands of steps long. O(V + E) time is expected.
sections.assumptions: Step names, durations and soak periods are invented. There is no limit on parallelism. An empty plan finishes at minute 0.
sections.criteria: Recognises a longest path in a DAG; Kahn's algorithm or an iterative DFS with three-state cycle detection; every edge relaxed once; handles isolated steps, an empty plan, self-dependencies and duplicate edges; no recursion-depth failure; O(V + E); at Very Hard, reconstructs the critical path with the stated tie rule.

clarifications.q: What if the dependencies contain a cycle?
clarifications.a: The rollout can never finish: return None. A step that depends on itself is a cycle.

clarifications.q: Are there limits on how many steps run at once?
clarifications.a: No. Only the dependencies constrain the schedule.

clarifications.q: What is the finish time of the whole rollout?
clarifications.a: The latest finish time of any step, including steps with no dependencies at all.

clarifications.q: Can a step depend on several others?
clarifications.a: Yes. It starts when the last of them allows it to.

clarifications.q: Will the input be small enough for recursion?
clarifications.a: No. Expect a chain of 30 000 steps; Python's default recursion limit is about 1 000.

hints: A step's earliest start is the maximum, over its dependencies, of that dependency's finish time (plus any soak). That is a longest-path problem, which is easy on a DAG and meaningless with a cycle.
Kahn's algorithm: count incoming edges, start from the steps with none, and release a step when its count reaches zero. If you process fewer steps than exist, there is a cycle.
Relax each edge once, in topological order: start[b] = max(start[b], finish[a] + soak).
For the critical path, record for each step which successor (or predecessor) achieves the maximum, and apply the tie rule when two do.
followups: Which steps have slack, and how much? Compute the latest start time of every step that does not delay the rollout.
Only 4 GPU pools can be updated at the same time. Does your algorithm still give the finish time? What kind of problem is it now?
The plan changes while the rollout is running: a step takes twice as long as planned. How do you recompute the finish time incrementally instead of from scratch?
The plan lives in a database and is edited by several teams. How would you reject a cyclic edit at write time, cheaply?

rules.ask: The input contains a 30 000-step chain. What does Python do, and how do you make the traversal iterative?
How many passes does repeated relaxation need in the worst case, and what is its total cost at 200 000 edges?
Dijkstra finds shortest paths with non-negative weights. Why is it not the right tool for the longest path here, and what does a DAG give you instead?
A step reachable along two paths is visited twice. How do you tell a harmless revisit from a cycle?
Where exactly does alphabetical order enter your algorithm, and does it change the finish time?

templates.title: Debug the hourly token usage rollup

sections.scenario: A usage service turns raw API usage events into per-project hourly token totals that feed the usage dashboard. On {{day}}, projects {{projects}} reported that the dashboard disagrees with their own request logs: some hours are too high, some requests appear in the wrong hour, and the totals drift upwards the longer the service runs. You are handed the function below.
sections.problem: The starter code is hourly_tokens(events), and it has several bugs. Fix it so that it meets this specification. Each event is a dict with request_id, project_id, attempt, ts_ms (epoch milliseconds, UTC), status, prompt_tokens and completion_tokens. A request can be retried; each retry is a new event with a higher attempt, and events arrive in any order. (1) For each request_id, only the event with the highest attempt counts. (2) The request is billed only if that event's status is "ok"; other statuses ("error", "timeout", "cancelled") bill nothing. (3) Its tokens (prompt_tokens + completion_tokens) go to the UTC hour containing ts_ms: the hour [h, h + 1 hour), where an event exactly on the hour belongs to the hour that starts then. (4) Return [(project_id, hour_start_epoch_seconds, tokens)] sorted by project, then hour, with no rows for hours that bill nothing. (5) Each call depends only on its own input. Explain each bug you find.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 events per call; one pass plus a sort is expected. An exact duplicate delivery of the same attempt can occur; (request_id, attempt) otherwise identifies one event.
sections.assumptions: The event shape and every value are hypothetical. Token counts are non-negative integers. All timestamps are UTC; there is no local time anywhere in the specification.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains all five bugs (first-seen deduplication, incomplete status filter, filtering before deduplication, the hour-boundary off-by-one, the mutable default argument); fixes them without new bugs; keeps a single pass; handles out-of-order attempts and exact duplicates; proposes tests that would have caught each bug.

clarifications.q: If attempt 1 succeeded and attempt 2 failed, is anything billed?
clarifications.a: No. The highest attempt decides; attempt 2 failed, so the request bills nothing.

clarifications.q: Which events count as billable?
clarifications.a: Only status "ok" on the request's latest attempt.

clarifications.q: Which hour does an event at exactly 10:00:00.000 belong to?
clarifications.a: The 10:00 hour. Hours are half-open, [h, h + 1 hour).

clarifications.q: Is the function called more than once in the same process?
clarifications.a: Yes, many times; it runs inside a long-lived service.

clarifications.q: Can the same attempt be delivered twice?
clarifications.a: Yes, as an exact duplicate. Count it once.

hints: Read the deduplication loop and ask: when two events share a request_id, which one survives, and does that depend on arrival order?
Should the status filter run before deduplication or after it? Try a request whose latest attempt failed.
Work out the bucket for ts_ms = 10 × 3 600 000 by hand.
Look at the function's signature. What is shared between calls?
followups: Write the smallest set of unit tests that would have caught every one of these bugs before they shipped.
Events now arrive as a stream, and an attempt can show up hours after the request. How do you keep the hourly totals correct without holding every event in memory?
The dashboard must show the project's local time zone. Where do you convert, and what happens to hours on days when clocks change?
Finance wants these totals to reconcile with billing to the token. Which of these bugs would also have broken billing, and how would a reconciliation job have detected each one?

rules.ask: Events arrive in any order. What does "last seen wins" do when attempt 3 arrives before attempt 2?
Does your status check run before or after you pick the latest attempt, and which test case tells the two apart?
An event at exactly midnight UTC: which day and hour does your code give it, and which does the old code give it?
Why does this bug only appear in a long-running service and never in a unit test that calls the function once?
Which time zone does that call use when you do not pass one, and would your tests catch it on a machine set to UTC?

templates.title: Exactly-once usage metering from inference events to billing

sections.scenario: Every completed API request emits a usage event: request_id, project_id, model, prompt and completion tokens, and a timestamp. Usage is billed per token, so each event must reach the billing ledger exactly once. Inference servers retry delivery when the log does not acknowledge, so about {{retry_share}} of events arrive more than once. Peak traffic is {{peak_rate}} events per second, the log topic has {{partitions}} partitions, and events can arrive up to {{lateness}} late after a regional outage.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the usage-event log to the billing ledger. Cover: the event contract and key; how the consumer processes events and commits offsets; what happens when a consumer crashes after writing to the ledger but before committing its offset; how the sink stays idempotent; how you replay a time range safely; how you reconcile the ledger against the raw log; and the cost of the deduplication state.
sections.constraints: The billing ledger must count every request exactly once, to the token. The usage dashboard may lag by a few minutes; the invoice may not be wrong. The ledger is an append-friendly store that supports conditional writes (insert if absent) or transactions. Consumers can be restarted, rescheduled or rebalanced at any time.
sections.assumptions: All rates, partition counts and lateness bounds are hypothetical. The log is Kafka-style: partitioned, ordered within a partition, at-least-once delivery to consumers, with consumer-group offsets.
sections.criteria: States precisely where exactly-once holds; idempotent ledger writes keyed by request_id (with a version for corrections); safe ordering of write and offset commit and a clear crash walk-through; bounded, sized deduplication state with a retention rule tied to lateness; replay and correction as new ledger entries, never silent rewrites; a reconciliation job at the request grain with alerting; aware of hot keys and rebalances.

clarifications.q: Is request_id unique across all regions and retries?
clarifications.a: Yes. A retry reuses the same request_id; a new request gets a new one.

clarifications.q: Can token counts for a request change after it is first reported?
clarifications.a: Rarely: a correction event with the same request_id and a higher version supersedes the earlier one.

clarifications.q: Does billing need per-request rows or only totals?
clarifications.a: Invoices use daily totals per project and model, but support must be able to explain any total down to its requests.

clarifications.q: Can I rely on the log's exactly-once (transactional) mode?
clarifications.a: Only between the log and itself. The ledger is an external store.

clarifications.q: How long must you be able to replay?
clarifications.a: At least the {{lateness}} lateness window, plus time to notice and fix a bug.

hints: Exactly-once end to end is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent effect. Decide where the idempotence lives.
If the ledger write and the offset commit cannot be atomic, make the write safe to repeat: a write keyed by request_id that is a no-op the second time.
Deduplication state is a set of keys you have seen. How long must you keep a key, and how large is that set at {{peak_rate}} events per second?
followups: A consumer writes 5 000 rows to the ledger and crashes before committing its offset. Walk through exactly what happens after restart.
Why does keying the topic by request_id (or project_id) matter, and what does each choice cost you?
A bug double-counted completion tokens for two hours last week, and invoices already went out. How do you correct the ledger, and how do you replay without double billing?
Size the deduplication state for the {{lateness}} window at peak, and propose a cheaper design that is still exact.
Design the reconciliation job that proves the ledger matches the raw log every day. What does it compare, at which grain, and what happens when it fails?

rules.ask: Your log's transactions cover the log. Where does that guarantee end, and what makes the write to the external ledger safe beyond that point?
A Bloom filter has false positives. What does a false positive do to an invoice, and is that acceptable here?
One project produces 20% of all usage. What happens to its partition at peak, and does that change your deduplication?
Two consumers race to write the same request_id after a rebalance. Show that your write is still correct.
If the offset is committed before the write and the consumer then crashes, which events are lost and who notices?

templates.title: Evaluation results ingestion pipeline

sections.scenario: Researchers evaluate model checkpoints against benchmark datasets. Each evaluation run scores every example in a dataset and writes per-example results; about {{runs_per_day}} runs a day, each over up to {{examples_per_run}} examples. Run metadata (checkpoint, dataset version, grader, configuration, status) lives in an experiment-tracking database; per-example scores are written as files to object storage. The metric payload has changed shape {{metric_versions}} times as graders evolved, and runs are often rerun up to {{rerun_window}} later after a grader fix.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that ingests evaluation results into an analytics store, so that researchers can compare checkpoints on the same dataset version and slice results by example attributes. Cover: change data capture from the experiment-tracking database; joining run metadata with per-example files; dataset and model versioning; schema evolution of the metric payload; late reruns and how they replace or sit beside earlier results; and how any number on a leaderboard can be reproduced later.
sections.constraints: A comparison between two checkpoints must only use results on the same dataset version with the same grader version. A run's results become visible only once the run is complete. Any published comparison must be reproducible exactly, months later. The tracking database is a production OLTP system and must not be loaded by analytics queries.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and version counts are hypothetical. The tracking database supports logical replication (a change log). Per-example files may arrive before or after the run's status changes to complete.
sections.criteria: Uses CDC (not polling) for run metadata and handles redelivery and ordering; gates visibility on run completion and on file arrival; immutable per-example facts keyed by run_id with explicit supersession for reruns; dataset and grader versions as first-class keys; a schema-evolution strategy with a registry and typed projections; a layout that serves checkpoint comparisons; a reproducibility record for every published number.

clarifications.q: Is a rerun a new run or an update to the old one?
clarifications.a: A new run_id that points to the run it replaces. Both must remain queryable.

clarifications.q: Can a dataset change after it is published?
clarifications.a: Never in place. A fix creates a new dataset version with its own id and content hash.

clarifications.q: Do metric payloads share one schema?
clarifications.a: No. Each grader declares a schema version; fields are added, renamed and occasionally change type.

clarifications.q: Who reads the results?
clarifications.a: Researchers in notebooks and dashboards, and an automated leaderboard that must be reproducible.

clarifications.q: Can a run be deleted?
clarifications.a: It can be marked invalid (for example a broken grader); its data stays for audit.

hints: Separate immutable facts (per-example scores of one run) from mutable state (a run's status, whether it is the current result for its checkpoint and dataset).
CDC gives you every change to run metadata in commit order. Think about what a "run completed" event should trigger, and what to do when files are not there yet.
Reproducibility means pinning everything a number depends on: checkpoint, dataset version and hash, grader version, configuration and the code that aggregated it.
followups: A grader bug inflated one metric for a week. How do you find every affected leaderboard number, and what do readers see after the rerun?
A grader renames pass to passed and changes score from integer to float. How does ingestion behave, and how do queries across versions keep working?
The per-example table reaches tens of billions of rows. How do you lay it out so a two-checkpoint comparison on one dataset reads only what it needs?
A CDC connector falls behind by six hours and then replays. What can go wrong with run status, and how do you make the consumer safe to replay?
Researchers want a leaderboard number from three months ago reproduced exactly, but the aggregation code has changed since. What did your design store to make that possible?

rules.ask: A published comparison used the old results. After your overwrite, how would anyone reproduce it?
The connector restarts and redelivers changes. How does your consumer stay correct when it sees the same run update twice, or out of order?
Keeping payloads schemaless defers the problem. Where are types finally enforced, and who learns when a grader breaks a field?
Most queries filter by dataset version and checkpoint, not by date. What does your partitioning cost those queries?
The tracking database is production OLTP. What load does polling put on it, and what does polling miss that CDC would not?

templates.title: Usage metering and billing data model

sections.scenario: A model API bills about {{orgs}} organizations. An organization owns projects; a project owns API keys; every request is made with one key. Usage is priced per SKU: a model with a unit such as input tokens, cached input tokens, output tokens, images or audio seconds. There are about {{skus}} SKUs across several model families, and list prices change several times a year, sometimes for one SKU in the middle of a month. Organizations receive credits (promotional and prepaid) and a monthly free-tier allowance on some SKUs, and are invoiced monthly in {{currencies}}. The metering pipeline produces about {{daily_lines}} usage records a day.
sections.problem: Design the data model behind metering and billing: (1) the transactional (system-of-record) model that prices usage, applies free-tier allowances and credits, and issues invoices; (2) the analytical (warehouse) model finance and product teams query. Name every entity with its keys, state the grain of every fact table, show how a price change takes effect, and explain how an invoice issued last month can be reproduced exactly, line by line, a year from now.
sections.constraints: An issued invoice is never edited; corrections must be visible as corrections. Money is never stored as a binary float. Any usage record must be traceable to the price row that rated it. Analysts must be able to answer "what did organization X spend on model family Y last quarter" without reading raw usage records.
sections.assumptions: All counts, prices and volumes are hypothetical. The usage record already carries a unique request id, the key, the SKU, the quantity and the UTC event time; deduplication of usage happens upstream.
sections.criteria: Clean separation of usage, pricing, allowances, credits and invoices; effective-dated, non-overlapping price rows with half-open intervals; rated lines carry the applied price id; credits as an append-only ledger with expiry; immutable invoices with adjustment lines; facts with explicitly stated grains; SCD choices justified for organization, project and key; decimal or minor-unit money; handles each incident with diagnosis, correction and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a project move to a different organization?
clarifications.a: Yes, rarely (after an acquisition). Usage before the move belongs to the old organization.

clarifications.q: When a price changes mid-month, which price applies?
clarifications.a: The price in effect at the request's event time; a month can contain both prices.

clarifications.q: In which order are free tier, credits and paid usage applied?
clarifications.a: Free-tier allowance first, then credits, then the remainder is billed. State the order in your model.

clarifications.q: Do credits expire?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each grant has an expiry date; unused credit is lost at expiry.

clarifications.q: Can a price differ per organization?
clarifications.a: Most organizations pay list price; a few enterprise contracts have negotiated rates with their own effective dates.

hints: Separate the facts that happened (a request consumed N units) from the decisions applied to them (which price, which allowance, which credit).
A price is a fact about time: give it an effective_from and a way to find the row in effect at any instant, and never update a price row in place.
Credits behave like a ledger of grants, consumptions and expiries, not like a balance column.
followups: Finance asks for revenue by model family by day. Which table answers it, at what grain, and how do you keep it consistent with the invoices?
A negotiated rate is signed today but backdated to the start of the month. What changes in your model, and what happens to invoices already issued?
A key is reassigned from one project to another mid-month. Show how usage before and after the move is attributed, in both the transactional and the analytical model.
At {{daily_lines}} records a day, which tables are partitioned and clustered how, and which aggregates do you precompute? What keeps the precomputed aggregates correct when a late record arrives?
A regulator asks you to prove that every invoiced amount came from metered usage at a published price. What query or artifact produces that proof?

rules.ask: Two price rows for one SKU overlap by one hour because of a data-entry error. What does your model do at request time, and what constraint would have stopped it?
Two invoices consume credit from the same grant at the same moment. How does a balance column stay correct, and how would a ledger change that?
What goes wrong when you sum a billion small amounts held as binary floats, and what type would you use instead?
A price was cut on the 15th. What does your query charge for usage on the 3rd?
Which of your dimensions change over time, and which SCD type does each one get?

incidents: A price cut for one SKU was entered with effective_from at local midnight instead of UTC midnight. For the first 8 hours of the month that SKU was rated at the old price, and invoices for several thousand of the {{orgs}} organizations have already been issued.

An enterprise customer disputes an invoice: the dashboard shows 3% less spend than the invoice for the same month. The dashboard reads the warehouse; the invoice was generated from the transactional model.
A metering replay delivers one hour of usage records a second time, and the duplicates reach the rating step for a subset of the {{daily_lines}} daily records.

templates.title: Event schema and data contract for multimodal requests

modalities: text, image and audio inputs and audio outputs

sections.scenario: A model API accepts requests made of ordered parts: {{modalities}}. Each request produces a telemetry event that {{consumers}} downstream teams consume: billing, capacity planning, product analytics, reliability and safety operations. {{producers}} services emit these events (gateways in different regions, a batch endpoint, a realtime endpoint), written in different languages and released on different schedules. About {{daily_events}} events a day.
sections.problem: Design the event schema and the data contract. Show the envelope and the per-part structure, with types and units. Classify every field into privacy tiers and say which tiers may enter the analytics platform, which stay in the serving path, and which are never stored. Define the versioning and compatibility rules, how a producer proves it honours the contract before release, and what happens at runtime to an event that breaks it.
sections.constraints: Request and response content (text, image bytes, audio, transcripts, file names) must never be written to telemetry. Consumers upgrade on their own schedules, so a new producer version must not break an old consumer. Billing needs per-part units exactly; other consumers can tolerate sampling.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, team counts and release cadence are hypothetical. A schema registry and a message log already exist; you design what goes in them.
sections.criteria: Consumer-driven field list; envelope plus ordered parts with explicit units; per-field tier annotations enforced by tooling; content excluded at the producer by an allow-list; keyed pseudonymisation for end-user ids; backward and forward compatibility rules with semantic versioning of meaning, not just shape; contract tests in producer CI plus runtime validation with a quarantine that does not lose billing units; adapts to each incident.

clarifications.q: Can analytics see the end user's identifier that a customer passes with a request?
clarifications.a: Only in a form that cannot be reversed or joined to other datasets; decide which form and who holds the key.

clarifications.q: Do consumers need image dimensions or audio length?
clarifications.a: Capacity planning needs pixel counts and audio seconds because they drive cost; exact values are fine, content is not.

clarifications.q: Who owns the schema?
clarifications.a: The serving platform team owns the producer side; each consumer team signs up to a versioned contract.

clarifications.q: Can a new modality appear?
clarifications.a: Yes. Video input is planned next year.

clarifications.q: What about safety classifications of the content?
clarifications.a: A category label and score per request may be stored in a restricted tier; the content they were computed from may not.

hints: Start from the consumers: list what each one needs, then derive the fields. Anything nobody needs is not collected.
Tag every field with a tier in the schema itself, so tooling can enforce it, rather than in a wiki page.
Think about what happens to an enum when a new value appears and an old consumer reads it.
followups: A product team asks for a hash of the prompt text so they can count repeated prompts. Is that content? What would you offer instead?
Walk through adding video input: the schema change, the compatibility mode, and what each existing consumer sees on day one.
A producer in one region starts sending audio_ms where the contract says audio_seconds. Where is it caught, by whom, and what happens to the events already written?
At {{daily_events}} events a day, how do you validate every event without adding latency to the request path?
How do you prove, to an auditor, that no content has reached analytics in the last 90 days?

rules.ask: A free-form attributes map is convenient. How does it interact with your privacy tiers and with the contract test?
An unsalted hash of a short prompt can be reversed by guessing. What makes a hash safe here, and who holds the key?
An old consumer reads an enum value it was compiled without. What happens, and how did you design for it?
Which compatibility mode do you set on the subject, and what change does it still allow that would break a consumer semantically?
Billing needs every event. If you reject a non-conforming event, how does billing still get its units?

incidents: A new SDK version adds a filename field on image parts. File names contain people's names, and the field has reached the analytics tables of all {{consumers}} consumer teams for 2 days.
One of the {{producers}} producing services renames audio_seconds to audio_ms in a "minor" release. The audio usage dashboard jumps 1000× for one region, and billing has already rated a day of it.
A realtime endpoint begins emitting one event per streamed chunk instead of one per request, and event volume triples overnight from {{daily_events}} a day.

templates.title: Warehouse model for model-evaluation results

graders: exact match, model graders and human raters

sections.scenario: A model provider evaluates every model version against about {{suites}} evaluation datasets (reasoning, coding, safety, multilingual, regression). Each example in a dataset is answered by the model, possibly several times, and scored by one or more graders: {{graders}}. About {{releases}} candidate versions are evaluated a month and the warehouse receives about {{results}} graded results a month. Release reviews compare a candidate against the current production model and against last quarter's model.
sections.problem: Design the warehouse model for evaluation results. Cover model versions, dataset versions, examples, runs, samples, graders and metrics. State the grain of every fact. Show how the model guarantees that two versions are compared fairly, how a late re-grade (a grader fixed weeks later) enters without silently changing published numbers, and how any published score can be reproduced exactly.
sections.constraints: A published score never changes in place. Datasets are edited over time (examples added, removed, relabelled). A comparison must be explainable down to the examples that differ. Raw model outputs may contain sensitive material and live in a restricted store; the warehouse holds identifiers and scores.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, counts and cadence are hypothetical. Evaluation runs themselves are scheduled by another system; you model what they produce.
sections.criteria: Immutable versioned dimensions (model version with decoding config, dataset version with example membership, example revision, grader version, metric definition); facts at stated grains (sample, grade, metric value); comparisons restricted to paired examples with matching grader versions; re-grades appended and selected by metric definition, not by recency; published scores as frozen snapshots with a manifest; statistical uncertainty; restricted outputs kept out of the warehouse; adapts to each incident.

clarifications.q: Do two dataset versions share example ids?
clarifications.a: Yes. An unchanged example keeps its id across versions; an edited one gets a new revision.

clarifications.q: Can one result have several grades?
clarifications.a: Yes: one per grader version, and graders are re-run when they are fixed.

clarifications.q: Are model outputs deterministic?
clarifications.a: No. Sampling settings vary, and even greedy decoding is not guaranteed bit-for-bit on accelerators, so some suites run several samples per example.

clarifications.q: Who decides which grader version counts?
clarifications.a: Each metric definition names its grader version; changing it is a reviewed change.

clarifications.q: How long are results kept?
clarifications.a: Indefinitely for scores; raw outputs follow the restricted store's retention.

hints: Make every input to a score a versioned, immutable dimension, then a run is just a combination of versions.
Fair comparison is about the intersection: the same examples, the same grader version, the same decoding settings.
Separate "a grade was recorded" from "this grade is the one the metric uses".
followups: Write the query shape that compares two model versions on one suite, restricted to examples both were graded on with the same grader version. What does it return when the overlap is small?
A grader bug is fixed and 30% of last month's results are re-graded. Show what changes in which tables, and what the release-review dashboard shows the next morning.
Leadership wants one number per model version. How do you aggregate across {{suites}} datasets without letting the largest dataset dominate, and how do you show uncertainty?
A dataset turns out to contain examples that also appear in a training set (contamination). How does the model let you recompute every past comparison without them?

rules.ask: A score published in last month's release review was computed with the old grade. After your update, can you still reproduce it?
Suite A has 40 examples and suite B has 40 000. What does your average mean, and what would you report instead?
Two dataset versions differ by 200 relabelled examples. How does a comparison between models evaluated on different versions stay fair?
Raw outputs are restricted. Which of your tables may hold them, and how does an analyst debug a regression without reading them?

incidents: A dataset was edited in place (3% of labels fixed) without a new version. Scores for the last {{releases}} releases were computed against different labels and appear in the same chart.
A model grader was upgraded and only half of this month's runs were re-graded. The release dashboard mixes grader versions and shows a 4-point regression that does not exist.
Two shards of one run were loaded twice after a retry, and one suite's pass rate is computed over duplicated results.

templates.title: Rate-limit and quota configuration model

dimensions: requests per minute and tokens per minute
requests per minute, tokens per minute and a daily token budget
requests per minute, tokens per minute, images per minute and a batch queue limit

sections.scenario: A model API limits usage with {{dimensions}}, per organization and per model family. Organizations sit in one of {{tiers}} usage tiers that rise automatically with spend and payment history; support can grant overrides (some temporary, for a launch week), and organizations can set lower caps on individual projects. About {{orgs}} organizations exist, and gateways look up limits about {{lookups}}. Reliability engineers and analysts want to know, for any throttled request, which limit applied and why.
sections.problem: Design the configuration model: tiers and their default limits, tier assignments, overrides, project caps, and the audit history of every change. Define how the effective limit for (organization, project, model family, dimension) is resolved, how the gateway gets it at request time without a database read per request, and how analysts reconstruct the limit that applied at any past instant, including after a correction was backdated.
sections.constraints: A project cap can only lower a limit, never raise it. Every change records who made it, when, why and the previous value. A gateway must keep serving if the configuration service is unavailable. An expired temporary override must stop applying on time.
sections.assumptions: Counts, rates and tier numbers are hypothetical. The limiting algorithm itself (sliding window, token bucket) is out of scope; you design the data it reads.
sections.criteria: Normalised configuration (tiers, tier limits, assignments, overrides, project caps) with explicit precedence; bitemporal history (valid time and recorded time) in an append-only change log; resolved, versioned snapshots pushed to gateways with last-known-good fallback; gateways log the snapshot version; expiry enforced at evaluation time, not by a cleanup job; analytics joins throttling events to the logged version; sizing; adapts to each incident.

clarifications.q: If an organization has an override and moves up a tier, which wins?
clarifications.a: The higher of the two, unless the override is marked as a ceiling. Make the rule explicit in your model.

clarifications.q: Can a change take effect in the future?
clarifications.a: Yes. Support schedules overrides for a launch date, with an end date.

clarifications.q: How fast must a change reach every gateway?
clarifications.a: Within 60 seconds for increases; decreases for abuse within 10 seconds.

clarifications.q: Are corrections ever backdated?
clarifications.a: Yes: a tier upgrade that should have happened last Tuesday is recorded today with last Tuesday's effective date.

clarifications.q: Do analysts need per-request limit values?
clarifications.a: They need to know, for a sample of throttled requests, the effective limit and which rule produced it.

hints: Two different times matter: when a rule is in effect, and when the system learned about it.
Precompute the resolved limit per key and ship versioned snapshots; let the gateway log the snapshot version it used.
Write the precedence rules as data or a small pure function that both the gateway and the analysts' views share.
followups: Write the lookup for "the effective tokens-per-minute limit for this project and model family at instant T, as the system knew it at instant K".
A temporary override ends at 00:00 UTC. Walk through every place the old value lives and how each one learns it has expired.
At {{lookups}}, what does the gateway hold in memory, how large is it for {{orgs}} organizations, and how is it updated incrementally?
An analyst finds throttling events where the logged limit does not match what your history table says. What are the possible causes, and which design choice makes this impossible?

rules.ask: The store is slow for 2 minutes. What limits does the gateway enforce during that window, and is that fail-open or fail-closed?
An analyst asks what the limit was last Tuesday at 14:00. Can your table still answer that?
A correction is backdated a week. How do you also answer "what did the gateway believe at the time"?
Show your precedence for one organization with a tier default, a temporary override and a project cap, and say what happens when the override expires.

incidents: A temporary override that ended at midnight stayed in the gateways' cache for 3 days, so one organization kept a 10× limit. With lookups running at {{lookups}}, nobody noticed until its invoice arrived.

A script backdated tier upgrades for 12 000 organizations by updating rows in place. Analysts' reports of which limit throttled which request changed overnight, and nobody can say what the gateways enforced last week.

The configuration snapshot grew past what gateways can load at startup after per-project caps were added for {{orgs}} organizations, and new gateway instances fail their readiness check during a traffic spike.

templates.title: Monthly cost per organization with prices that change mid-month
templates.subtopic: point-in-time joins, month grids, period-over-period change

sections.scenario: A model API bills organizations monthly. Usage is recorded per project and model in batches (usage_records); a project belongs to one organization. Model prices are effective-dated: model_prices holds one row per model per price, valid from its effective_from until the next row for that model. Organizations receive credits for a month (credits). Finance wants the organizations whose net monthly cost moved by more than {{threshold}}% against the previous month, for {{months_text}}.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month, org_id, prev_net_usd, net_usd, pct_change, status for the months starting {{m2}} and {{m3}} (each compared with the month before; the data starts at {{m1}}), ordered by month, org_id. The rules:

  • A usage row costs input_tokens × usd_per_mtok_input / 1 000 000 + output_tokens × usd_per_mtok_output / 1 000 000, at the price row in effect at its usage_ts: the row for that model with the latest effective_from <= usage_ts. {{price_note}}
  • month is the first day of the UTC calendar month of usage_ts. An organization's monthly gross is the exact sum over its projects, rounded to cents once. {{gap_note}}
  • net_usd = max(0, gross − credits for that organization and month). Unused credit does not carry over. {{credit_note}}
  • An organization-month is reported when the previous month's net is above 0 and |net − prev| × 100 > {{threshold}} × prev (strictly greater). Then pct_change = round(100 × (net − prev) / prev, 2) and status is UP or DOWN.
  • When the previous month's net is 0 and this month's is above 0, report it with pct_change NULL and status FROM_ZERO.
  • {{unpriced_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). PostgreSQL. The sample has {{usage_rows}} usage rows; production has hundreds of millions a month, so say how your query would scale.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, prices and volumes; prices are in US dollars per 1 million tokens. Every organization in organizations is billed, whether or not it has usage. Timestamps are UTC.
sections.criteria: Correct point-in-time price match with an inclusive effective_from; exact sum rounded once; credits aggregated before joining and net floored at 0; full organization × month grid; strict threshold; the stated rules for previous-month zero and unpriced usage; deterministic order; can discuss scale and retroactive corrections.

clarifications.q: A price row takes effect at 14:00:00 and a usage row is at exactly 14:00:00. Which price?
clarifications.a: The new one. A row is in effect from its effective_from, inclusive.

clarifications.q: Do I round each usage row to cents?
clarifications.a: No. Sum the exact amounts per organization and month, then round once to cents.

clarifications.q: Can credits exceed the month's cost?
clarifications.a: Yes. The net is floored at 0, and the unused credit is lost.

clarifications.q: Is the threshold inclusive?
clarifications.a: No. A change of exactly the threshold is not reported.

clarifications.q: What if the previous month's net is 0?
clarifications.a: The percentage is undefined: report FROM_ZERO when the current net is above 0, otherwise nothing.

hints: Price each usage row first. LEFT JOIN LATERAL (… WHERE effective_from <= usage_ts ORDER BY effective_from DESC LIMIT 1) is one way; turning the price rows into [effective_from, next effective_from) intervals with LEAD is another.
Aggregate usage and credits to organization × month separately, then join them. Joining credits to usage rows multiplies both.
Build the full organization × month grid before comparing months, so that a month without usage still exists (and costs 0).
followups: Rewrite the price lookup with LEAD intervals and a range join. Which version would you run over hundreds of millions of usage rows, and why?
A negotiated rate for one organization overrides list price for some models. Change the model and the query.
Finance asks why an organization's cost rose 40%. Decompose the change into volume, price and credit effects.
Prices are corrected retroactively (a typo in one row). How do you find every invoice the correction affects, and what do you issue?

rules.ask: A usage row lands exactly at a price change. Which price does your condition pick, and which should it?
An organization has usage in the first and third month but none in the second. What does your LAG compare the third month with?
An organization has two credit grants and forty usage rows in a month. How many times is each counted after your join?
Some usage has no price in effect. What does your join do with it, and does that match the stated rule?
Where exactly do you round, and how far can rounding each row drift from rounding the total over a million rows?

incidents: The price table is reloaded without its primary key, and one model gains a second row with the same effective_from and a different price. Depending on how the price is matched, that model's usage is double-counted or priced arbitrarily, and the {{threshold}}% alert fires for organizations whose usage did not change.
A month-end job ran before the last day's usage arrived, so the baseline month ({{m1}}) is short for some organizations and the next month shows false increases.

templates.title: Inference telemetry and usage analytics platform

sections.scenario: A model API serves {{families}} model families from {{regions}} regions. Every request emits telemetry: model, region, project, prompt and completion token counts, time to first token, total latency and outcome. About {{daily_events}} events arrive per day. Product teams want live dashboards; finance needs token totals that reconcile exactly with billing; on-call engineers need error-rate and p95 latency alerts within {{freshness}}.
sections.problem: Design the platform that ingests these events and serves: (1) token consumption per project, model family and hour; (2) error rate and p95 latency per model family and region with {{freshness}} freshness; (3) a daily usage feed that billing can reconcile against. Cover the event schema, ingestion, stream and batch processing, storage and serving, privacy controls and failure handling.
sections.constraints: Raw telemetry is kept for {{retention_days}} days. Prompt and completion content must never reach the analytics platform. Dashboards p95 under 1 second. Usage totals feeding billing must be exact; dashboards may be approximate if labelled.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and SLOs are hypothetical. Each region runs its own inference fleet and can be cut off from the others.
sections.criteria: Separates exact and approximate paths; event-time windows with an explicit lateness policy; mergeable percentile sketches; idempotent usage aggregation keyed by request_id; regional isolation with replay safety; content stripped at the producer under a data contract; costed storage tiers; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can dashboard numbers be approximate?
clarifications.a: Yes, if labelled; billing totals cannot.

clarifications.q: Is p95 per model family per region or global?
clarifications.a: Both. Per family per region for alerts, global for the executive view.

clarifications.q: How late can events arrive?
clarifications.a: Most within seconds; a region recovering from an outage can deliver hours of backlog.

clarifications.q: Does any team need per-request detail?
clarifications.a: Support needs to look up one request by request_id for {{retention_days}} days.

clarifications.q: Who owns the event schema?
clarifications.a: The inference platform team; analytics consumes it under a data contract.

hints: Separate the exact path (usage that feeds billing) from the approximate path (latency percentiles, live dashboards). They have different correctness and freshness needs.
p95 cannot be averaged across partitions or regions. Think about mergeable sketches.
Decide where content is stripped: at the producer, before anything is written.
followups: How do you compute p95 latency per family per region every 30 seconds, and how do you combine regions into a global p95 without shipping raw events?
A region is unreachable for 3 hours, then replays its backlog. What do the dashboards show during the outage, what happens to billing, and how do you prevent double counting on replay?
Billing's daily total and your dashboard disagree by 0.4% for one project. Walk through how you find out which one is wrong.
Your storage bill doubles in a quarter. Where is the money going, and what do you change without breaking the {{retention_days}}-day lookup?
A new model family emits a field the schema does not know. How does the platform behave, and who finds out?

rules.ask: One enterprise project sends 30% of all traffic. What happens to the partition and the consumer that owns it?
Your usage aggregation needs every event for a request_id handled once. How do you keep that guarantee with random partitioning?
Why can't the platform average per-partition p95 values to get a global p95?
Where exactly does your exactly-once guarantee end, and what makes the billing feed correct beyond that point?
The constraint says content must never reach analytics. Where in your design is content removed, and how would you prove it?

incidents: Traffic rises 20× within an hour after a launch: from {{daily_events}} per day to that rate times twenty. Consumer lag on the usage topic reaches 30 minutes.
A deploy adds the full prompt text to the telemetry payload by mistake, and it has been flowing for 40 minutes.
An upstream bug replays the last 6 hours of events from one region.
The daily usage feed and the billing system disagree for 1 project in {{regions}} regions.

templates.title: Batch inference job platform with a 24-hour completion window

sections.scenario: A model API offers an asynchronous batch endpoint at a lower price than synchronous calls. A customer uploads a file of up to {{max_requests}} requests (one JSON request per line, each with a customer-chosen custom_id), creates a batch against it, and gets back an output file of results and an error file of failed lines. The platform promises a 24-hour completion window; when the window closes, unfinished requests are not run, the batch is marked expired, and the results already produced are still delivered. Around {{daily_batches}} batches are created per day. The inference fleet in {{regions}} regions sizes for synchronous peaks, so roughly {{idle_share}} of its capacity sits idle outside peak hours, and batch work is meant to use that capacity without ever slowing synchronous traffic.
sections.problem: Design the batch platform end to end: file intake and validation, the job and request state model, scheduling onto spare capacity with the 24-hour deadline, retries, partial results and the output files, expiry and cancellation, and cost accounting so each customer is charged exactly once for each request that completed. Say how batch capacity is kept separate from synchronous traffic.
sections.constraints: A synchronous request must never wait behind batch work. Every completed request is billed once and only once, at the batch price; requests that never ran are not billed. Results must survive a worker or region failure. The window is 24 hours from batch creation and does not stretch.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, prices and capacity shares are hypothetical. The output format (one result per input line, matched by custom_id) is fixed by the public API; everything behind it is yours to design.
sections.criteria: Request-level state model with idempotent result commits; a scheduler that preempts for synchronous traffic and prioritises by deadline slack with per-customer fairness; explicit validation policy; partial results and expiry handled as first-class states; billing derived once from committed results keyed by (batch_id, line); capacity isolation and regional failure handled; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do results have to come back in input order?
clarifications.a: No. Each result line carries the custom_id; customers match on it.

clarifications.q: Can a batch be cancelled?
clarifications.a: Yes. Requests already running finish; the rest are not started; completed results are delivered.

clarifications.q: Is the 24-hour window a hard deadline or a target?
clarifications.a: Hard. At 24 hours the batch expires; you deliver what finished.

clarifications.q: Can batch work run in any region?
clarifications.a: Yes, unless the customer's project is pinned to one region for data residency.

clarifications.q: Does a single invalid line fail the whole file?
clarifications.a: Your call. Say what you choose and why.

hints: Treat the request (batch_id, line number) as the unit of scheduling, retry and billing, not the batch.
Spare capacity is a fluctuating supply. The scheduler needs a priority signal that synchronous traffic can preempt, and a notion of how far behind each batch is against its deadline.
Billing exactly once is easier if usage is derived from durable result records rather than from worker events.
followups: How does the scheduler decide which batch runs next when spare capacity is short? What do you do with a batch that will clearly miss its window?
A worker finishes a request, writes the result, then dies before acknowledging. How do you avoid running and billing it twice?
One customer submits {{max_requests}}-line batches all day and would take most of the spare capacity. How do you keep fairness across customers without wasting idle capacity?
Synchronous peak lasts longer than forecast and spare capacity drops to zero for most of a day. What happens to the batches already in flight, and what do customers see?
How would you price and plan capacity so the 24-hour promise holds for 99.9% of batches, and what metric tells you it is about to break?

rules.ask: When synchronous traffic preempts a batch request mid-generation, is the partial work lost? What does that do to your throughput and to billing?
A batch created at 09:00 with 100 lines sits behind one created at 08:55 with the maximum number of lines. Is FIFO still the right order with a 24-hour deadline?
Which failures do you retry, which go to the error file, and how do you stop a retried request being billed twice?
Name the key that makes a request's result and its charge idempotent, and where it is enforced.
A dedicated batch fleet sits idle at night like the synchronous one. How do you justify its cost against borrowing idle synchronous capacity?

incidents: A launch keeps synchronous traffic at peak for 14 hours, so the spare capacity batch normally borrows (about {{idle_share}} of the fleet) falls close to zero. At hour 20, 6% of batches created that morning are less than half complete.
A worker pool loses its result-commit acknowledgements for 40 minutes because of a storage throttle. Requests are retried, and the usage feed shows some requests counted twice for a few customers.
A customer uploads a {{max_requests}}-line file in which line 31,000 is not valid JSON. Their support ticket asks why nothing ran for 3 hours.
One of the {{regions}} regions is lost for 2 hours while it holds partly processed requests from about a fifth of the batches in flight.

templates.title: Evaluation platform for model release candidates

sections.scenario: A model provider runs a fixed set of {{suites}} benchmark suites against every release candidate before it ships: reasoning, coding, safety and regression suites, some scored by exact match, some by executing generated code in a sandbox and some by a grader model. About {{candidates}} candidates arrive per week, and the accelerator budget for evaluation is {{budget}} accelerator-hours per week. Release managers need every suite's result for a candidate within {{deadline}} of the checkpoint landing, and they compare each candidate with the current production model to decide whether it ships.
sections.problem: Design the evaluation platform: how a run is defined and orchestrated, how suites are scheduled onto accelerators within the budget and deadline, what is cached and on what key, how results are made reproducible and stored, and how two releases are compared fairly. Include cost accounting per run.
sections.constraints: A score is only comparable with another if every input that could change it is the same or recorded. Results are kept indefinitely; raw generations for 180 days. Grader-model calls and sandboxed code execution count against the same budget. A failed suite must not block the others.
sections.assumptions: Suite counts, budgets and deadlines are hypothetical. Suites differ by two orders of magnitude in cost.
sections.criteria: Run manifest that pins every score-affecting input; content-addressed caching invalidated by any of them; deadline- and budget-aware scheduling with partial failure isolated per suite; checkpointed or resumable suites on preemptible capacity; fair comparison on the same harness with confidence intervals; immutable result storage with lineage; per-run cost; handles each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Are generations sampled or greedy?
clarifications.a: Both: some suites sample several times per item and report a mean; others decode greedily.
