clarifications.q: Can a run be partially reused from a previous candidate?
clarifications.a: Only where nothing that affects the score changed. You define that.

clarifications.q: Who adds or changes a suite?
clarifications.a: Research teams, through a review. Changing a suite must not silently change history.

clarifications.q: Is the grader model fixed?
clarifications.a: It is versioned and changes a few times a quarter.

clarifications.q: What does the release manager see?
clarifications.a: Per-suite deltas against production with uncertainty, and a list of anything missing.

hints: Write down everything that defines a score: checkpoint, suite version, prompt template, decoding parameters, seeds, grader version, harness version. That tuple is your cache key and your reproducibility record.
Compare a candidate against production on the same harness and suite version; re-run the baseline when the harness changes rather than trusting a historical number.
Small suites have wide confidence intervals. A 1-point drop on 150 items may be noise.
followups: Walk through the scheduler: given the budget and {{deadline}}, which suites run first, and what happens when accelerators are short?
What exactly is the cache key for a suite result, and what invalidates it?
A safety suite shows a 3-point regression on the candidate. How does the platform help someone decide whether it is real?
Research wants to add a suite that costs as much as the rest combined. How do you decide whether it runs on every candidate?
Two teams report different scores for the same checkpoint on the same suite. Design the platform so this cannot happen silently.

rules.ask: The grader model was upgraded last night. Which cached results are still valid, and how does your key know?
A preemptible pool is reclaimed 70% through a long suite. Do you restart it, resume it, or score what finished?
How do you report the uncertainty on that mean, and how many items does a suite need before a 1-point delta means anything?
What is a node in your DAG, and how does one failed suite avoid failing the run?
The production model's score was computed four months ago on an older harness. Is the comparison fair?

incidents: A candidate drops 4 points on a coding suite. Two days later the cause is found: the harness upgraded its prompt template between the baseline run and the candidate run.
Grader-model results are served from cache after the grader was upgraded, so a third of the suites in this week's {{candidates}} runs were scored by the old grader.
A preemptible accelerator pool is reclaimed twice in one night; the run misses the {{deadline}} target and the release review starts with eleven suites missing.
The same checkpoint scored twice on a 200-item suite differs by 1.5 points with every recorded setting identical.

templates.title: Observability and capacity planning for a GPU inference fleet

sections.scenario: An inference fleet of {{nodes}} accelerator nodes across {{regions}} regions serves {{models}} models. Each node hosts replicas of one or more models; requests queue at a router, are batched on the node, run a prefill phase over the prompt and then decode tokens one at a time. The service level objective is p95 time to first token under {{ttft_slo}} per model per region. Operators need to know when the fleet is saturated, when a node is quietly failing, how many replicas to add before tomorrow's peak, and how many accelerators to order for next quarter.
sections.problem: Design the observability and capacity-planning system: which metrics are collected per node, per replica and per model; how they are shipped, stored and queried; which signals drive autoscaling; how hardware faults are detected and nodes drained; and how capacity forecasts are produced from the same data.
sections.constraints: Metrics must reach alerting within 30 seconds. The metrics system must stay up when the fleet is in trouble. Per-project labels are not allowed on fleet metrics (cardinality and privacy). Accelerators take weeks to procure, so forecasts drive real purchases.
sections.assumptions: Fleet size, model count and SLOs are hypothetical. Nodes expose accelerator health counters (temperature, memory errors, interconnect errors, throttling) through a vendor management library.
sections.criteria: Metric taxonomy covering demand, supply, saturation and health; TTFT decomposed into queue wait and prefill; autoscaling on queue-based signals with lead time for slow replica start; peer-relative outlier detection with automatic drain; cardinality budget and a two-tier metrics pipeline that survives incidents; forecasts in tokens by phase and model mix with headroom; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is accelerator utilization a good saturation signal?
clarifications.a: You tell me. The counter most fleets report is the fraction of time a kernel was running.

clarifications.q: Do models share nodes?
clarifications.a: Some small models share; large models span several accelerators on one node.

clarifications.q: How fast can a replica start?
clarifications.a: Several minutes, mostly loading weights.

clarifications.q: Who consumes the forecast?
clarifications.a: The capacity team, monthly, for purchase orders.

hints: Separate demand signals (arrivals, tokens requested) from supply signals (tokens per second served) and from saturation signals (queue depth, queue wait, KV-cache occupancy).
A slow node is harder to catch than a dead one. Compare each node with its peers serving the same model.
Time to first token mixes queue wait and prefill. Measure both.
followups: Which signal drives scale-up, which drives scale-down, and why not the same one?
Replicas take minutes to start. How does that change the autoscaling policy?
How do you detect a node that answers correctly but 40% slower than its peers, and what happens automatically?
How do you build next quarter's accelerator forecast from these metrics, and what would make it wrong?
The metrics store itself is overloaded during the worst incident of the year. What did you design so operators can still see the fleet?

rules.ask: The utilization counter reads near 100% both when batches are full and healthy and when requests are queueing. What signal tells those apart?
At this fleet size, what does tracing every request cost, and what do you sample instead?
Someone adds a per-project label to one histogram. What happens to series count and to the store?
Why can an average TTFT look healthy while p95 breaches the SLO?
A new model launches with prompts four times longer. How does your forecast account for a change in mix, not just volume?

incidents: p95 time to first token for one model in one region breaches {{ttft_slo}} for two hours while fleet-wide averages look normal. The cause is eight nodes whose accelerators are throttling on temperature.
The autoscaler, driven by accelerator utilization, never scales up during a launch because utilization was already near 100% at normal load. Queue wait grows to 20 seconds.
A deploy adds a per-endpoint label to the latency histogram across all {{nodes}} nodes; active series grow 40× and the metrics store starts dropping writes.
A new model with long prompts takes 30% of traffic in a week. Tokens per second per node look fine, but TTFT breaches the SLO at peak.

templates.title: Privacy and retention enforcement for telemetry and logs

sections.scenario: An AI API platform writes {{daily_volume}} a day of request telemetry and service logs. The data lands in a lakehouse (object storage with table formats that support row-level deletes and time travel), is copied into a warehouse for analytics, is cached in a few serving stores, and is backed up nightly with backups kept {{backup_days}} days. Policy defines retention tiers: operational logs for 14 days, standard telemetry for {{standard_days}} days, aggregated usage (no request detail) for 7 years, and a zero-retention tier for customers whose agreements say request detail must not be stored at all. Customers and the platform can also request deletion of a project's or an organisation's data, to be completed within {{deletion_sla}}.
sections.problem: Design how retention and deletion are enforced across every copy: classification and tagging at write time, retention enforcement per tier, deletion requests that reach the lake, warehouse, caches, derived tables and backups, an access audit trail, and evidence that deletion actually happened. Estimate what it costs and say where you would spend less.
sections.constraints: A deletion is not complete until no readable copy exists, including table-format snapshots kept for time travel. Backups cannot be rewritten record by record. The zero-retention tier must never be written to durable storage. Audit logs are themselves retained and must not contain request content.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, tiers and service levels are hypothetical. Every record carries an organisation id and a project id; some derived tables were built before that rule existed.
sections.criteria: Classification and tier tags assigned at write time and inherited through lineage; retention enforced per tier with positive monitoring (absence of old data is checked, not assumed); deletion workflow across lake, warehouse, caches, derived tables and snapshots, with backups handled by short retention or key destruction and a deletion ledger re-applied on restore; zero-retention enforced in the serving path; access audit with ticket references; per-request evidence of deletion; costed; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a deletion request cover derived aggregates?
clarifications.a: Aggregates with no request detail and no identifiers are out of scope; anything keyed by the project is in scope.

clarifications.q: How are zero-retention customers identified?
clarifications.a: A flag on the organisation, read at request time by the serving layer.

clarifications.q: Who can read raw telemetry?
clarifications.a: Named on-call and support roles, with a ticket reference. Everyone else uses aggregates.

clarifications.q: What counts as proof of deletion?
clarifications.a: That is part of what you design. Auditors will ask for it per request.

clarifications.q: Can a restore from backup happen?
clarifications.a: Yes, after corruption. Assume one restore a quarter.

hints: Deleting rows in a table format writes new files; the old files stay readable through snapshots until they are expired and removed.
If backups cannot be edited, either keep them short enough to age out within the service level, or make the data unreadable without a key you can destroy.
A deletion you cannot list the copies for is a deletion you cannot prove. Start from lineage.
followups: Walk one deletion request for a project from intake to the evidence you hand the auditor. Which systems does it touch, in what order?
Your backups are kept {{backup_days}} days and the deletion service level is {{deletion_sla}}. How do you reconcile them?
A restore from backup brings back last week's data. How do you stop deleted records coming back to life?
How do you make sure a new pipeline written next quarter inherits the right retention tier without anyone remembering to configure it?
What does this cost per month, and which control would you weaken first if finance asked for a 30% cut?

rules.ask: Where do the keys live, what happens to aggregate tables that mix projects, and how do you prove a key is really gone?
An object-storage lifecycle rule deletes old files, but the table metadata still references them. What do readers and time travel see?
How long does the soft-deleted data stay readable, and to whom?
What retention do you set on snapshots, and what does that cost you in rollback ability?
Your audit log records who queried which project. How long is it kept, and does keeping it conflict with a deletion request?

incidents: The daily retention job for the {{standard_days}}-day tier has been failing silently for 11 days after a table was renamed; nothing alerted.
A deletion request was marked complete within {{deletion_sla}}, but three weeks later the project's request detail is found in an analyst's scratch table in the warehouse.
A restore from a backup taken 9 days ago brings back data for two organisations whose deletion completed last week.
A serving-layer bug writes request detail for zero-retention customers into the operational log tier for 6 hours.

templates.title: Usage numbers that finance no longer trusts

sections.scenario: Your team owns the usage pipeline that turns inference telemetry into token totals. For {{days}} days, the totals have drifted {{drift}} above what the billing system charged. The number has already appeared in {{audience}}. The inference platform team says their events are correct; the billing team says the same about theirs.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would lead the response: the first hour, the first day and the following two weeks. Then tell me about a real time you led a team through a data-correctness problem that other teams disputed (use STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: You cannot pause billing. Three teams own parts of the path, and none reports to you.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical situation and figures.
sections.criteria: Contains first; verifies before asserting; brings three owners to one fact base at a shared grain; clear decision rights and communication to finance; blameless but accountable; concrete prevention with owners; real example has measurable evidence and a personal contribution, or is honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has anyone acted on the wrong number?
clarifications.a: Yes: it went into {{audience}}.

clarifications.q: Who decides what is published externally?
clarifications.a: Finance, with your recommendation.

clarifications.q: Is customer billing itself known to be wrong?
clarifications.a: Unknown. That is part of what you must establish.

hints: Contain before you diagnose: who needs to stop using the number right now?
Compare the three systems at the finest grain they share.
A good answer names who owns each decision and how disagreement gets resolved.
followups: The inference team's lead says the drift is your pipeline's bug and refuses to look. What do you do?
You find that both sides are partly wrong. How do you communicate that without making it a blame exercise?
What would you change so this class of problem is caught within an hour next time? Name the check, its threshold, where it runs and who is paged.
What did you personally do in your real example, separate from your team, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: How do you keep three teams cooperating once someone feels blamed?
What exactly would you roll back, and how do you know the rollback does not make billing worse?
What threshold would have fired here, and how do you stop it paging every day for noise?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Build or buy an evaluation platform under launch pressure

gap: it cannot run evaluations inside your own network
it has no way to version grader models

sections.scenario: A model launch is {{weeks}} weeks away. Research runs evaluations with a collection of scripts that nobody fully trusts, and leadership wants a proper evaluation platform before the launch. You lead a team of {{team}} engineers. A vendor offers a hosted evaluation product for about {{vendor_cost}} a year that covers most needs, but {{gap}}. Your team estimates a minimal in-house platform at most of the time before launch, with nothing else delivered in that period.
sections.problem: How would you reach and drive the decision: what you would find out in the first days, who decides, what you would recommend under each outcome, and how you would protect the launch either way? Then tell me about a real build-versus-buy or adopt-versus-extend decision you drove (STAR, with what it cost and what happened afterwards), or say plainly that you have not and reason through it.
sections.constraints: The launch date does not move. Evaluation results gate the launch. The team cannot grow before launch.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical situation, prices and estimates. No real vendor is implied.
sections.criteria: Frames the decision around the launch's real requirements and the long-term platform separately; gathers evidence fast (vendor proof of concept on the hardest requirement, security review started on day one, honest in-house estimate); prices both options including opportunity cost and year-two ownership; names the decider and records the decision; keeps a fallback for the launch; protects reversibility by owning formats and data; real example has evidence, a personal contribution and lessons, or is honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Who signs the vendor contract?
clarifications.a: Your director, on your recommendation, after a security review that takes about three weeks.

clarifications.q: Can the existing scripts run the launch evaluations?
clarifications.a: Yes, with heroics. Their results have disagreed with each other twice this quarter.

clarifications.q: What does research want most?
clarifications.a: Results they can reproduce and compare, more than a dashboard.

hints: Separate what must be true for the launch from what the platform should become afterwards.
Price the in-house option in engineer-weeks and in what does not get done, not only in salary.
Make the decision reversible where you can: what would you need to own so switching later is cheap?
followups: Research leadership prefers to build because "evaluation is our core competency". Your estimate says building puts the launch at risk. How do you handle that conversation?
You choose the vendor, and five weeks before launch the security review finds a blocker. What is your fallback, and when did you prepare it?
How would you write the decision down so that someone reading it in a year understands why it was right or wrong at the time?
In your real example, what evidence did you have, what did you get wrong, and what did it cost?

rules.ask: Which part of evaluation is actually differentiating, and could you build only that part and buy the rest?
What exactly would you own (manifests, result formats, data) so leaving the vendor later is cheap?
Walk me through the in-house number. What is the on-call and maintenance cost in year two?
What did you personally recommend, and what would have changed your mind?

templates.title: Telemetry storage and query costs doubled in a quarter
templates.subtopic: storage and compute, cross-team cost ownership

driver: a dashboard tool that rescans raw tables every few minutes
a new debugging dataset nobody set a retention for
traffic that grew three-fold after a launch

sections.scenario: The telemetry platform your team owns costs {{spend}} a month in storage and query compute, double what it cost a quarter ago. Finance has asked for a {{target}} reduction within {{deadline}} without losing anything the business depends on. Your first look suggests one large contributor is {{driver}}, but most of the bill is not yet attributed to any team.
sections.problem: How would you lead this: what you would do in the first week, how you would decide what to cut, how you would bring the teams that create the cost along, and how you would keep it from doubling again? Then describe a real cost reduction you led (STAR, with the before and after numbers and your own part), or say plainly that you have not and reason through it.
sections.constraints: Billing-grade usage data and its daily reconciliation must not be affected. You do not control the teams that run most of the queries.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical figures and causes.
sections.criteria: Attributes cost before cutting; unit economics and a ranked list of savings with estimates; quick engineering wins separated from behaviour changes that need negotiation; protects billing-grade data; makes cost visible to the teams that cause it (showback or budgets) with an owner; verifies savings and checks for harm; real example has before and after numbers and a personal contribution, or is honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can you see who runs which queries?
clarifications.a: Query logs exist, but most dashboards use one shared service account.

clarifications.q: Is the growth in traffic itself expected to continue?
clarifications.a: Yes. Unit cost has to fall even if total cost does not.

clarifications.q: Is anyone already accountable for cost?
clarifications.a: No team has a cost budget for data today.

hints: You cannot cut what you cannot attribute. Unit costs (per million events stored, per query, per dashboard) beat a total.
Some savings are pure engineering (formats, partitioning, compaction, retention); some need someone else to change behaviour. Plan them differently.
Decide in advance how you will know a cut did no harm.
followups: A research team's ad-hoc queries are 30% of compute, and their lead says the work is critical and the cost is not your concern. What do you do?
Shortening retention would meet the target on its own. Why might that be the wrong first move?
How do you stop costs drifting up again next year? Name the mechanism and who owns it.
In your real example, which saving did you expect that never materialised, and why?

rules.ask: Who depends on the oldest data today, and how did you find out before cutting it?
How do you make attribution fair when shared tables serve several teams?
How much of the target does that deliver, and how did you estimate it before doing the work?
Which consumers can live with sampled data, and how do you keep billing-grade data exact?

templates.title: A legacy metering job, one owner, who is leaving
templates.subtopic: bus factor, safe migration of billing-critical code

stack: a chain of shell scripts and SQL files run by cron
a single 6,000-line Python script on one virtual machine
an old Spark job pinned to a framework version nobody else uses

sections.scenario: A nightly metering job turns usage records into the per-customer totals that invoices are built from, about {{volume}} of revenue a month. It is {{stack}}, has no tests, and is understood by one engineer, who has resigned and leaves in {{weeks_left}} weeks. Invoices are generated on {{invoice_day}} of each month. Your roadmap for the quarter is already full.
sections.problem: What do you do this week, before the engineer leaves, and over the next two quarters? Who do you involve, what do you stop, and how do you replace the job without changing a single invoice by accident? Then describe a real time you inherited or retired critical code with little knowledge transfer (STAR, with measurable outcomes and your own part), or say plainly that you have not and reason through it.
sections.constraints: Invoices must go out on {{invoice_day}} every month. Any change to totals must be explained to finance before an invoice carries it.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical system, timing and figures.
sections.criteria: Treats the departure as a risk with a deadline and acts this week (recorded walkthroughs, runbook tested by someone else running the job, access and credentials transferred, the manual adjustments explained); makes the risk visible and trades roadmap explicitly; replaces the job through characterisation tests and a parallel run compared at customer and line grain; agrees with finance how intentional differences are handled; spreads ownership; real example has evidence, a personal contribution and lessons, or is honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the leaving engineer cooperative?
clarifications.a: Yes, but busy with their own handover list.

clarifications.q: Are there known bugs?
clarifications.a: Two customers' totals are adjusted by hand every month. Nobody knows why.

clarifications.q: Can you add headcount?
clarifications.a: Not this quarter. You can trade roadmap items with your manager's approval.

hints: Before rewriting anything, capture what the job actually does: inputs, outputs, schedules, and the manual steps around it.
A parallel run with automated comparison is the safest way to prove a replacement.
Ask what you are willing to drop from the roadmap. The answer is the real priority.
followups: Two weeks into the parallel run, the new job differs from the old one by 0.3% for twelve customers. The old job's behaviour looks like a bug. Which one goes on the invoice?
Your manager wants to delay the rewrite to next year because "it has run for five years". How do you make the case, or do you agree?
How do you make sure the knowledge does not end up in one new person's head?
In your real example, what did you discover only after the previous owner had gone?

rules.ask: How do you prove the rewrite produces the same totals, and what do you do where it should not?
What specifically goes in the runbook in the first week, and how do you test it before the owner leaves?
How long does the parallel run last, what is the comparison grain, and what difference is acceptable?
Headcount is frozen this quarter. What do you take off the roadmap instead?

templates.title: Request logging — research wants more, privacy wants less

ask: full request and response bodies for 30 days
a 5% sample of request and response bodies for 14 days
token-level output probabilities plus request metadata for 30 days

sections.scenario: Model researchers want richer request logging to debug quality regressions: {{ask}}. The privacy team wants less than is logged today, pointing to customer agreements and the data-minimisation principle. Infrastructure estimates the request at {{cost}} a month in storage and processing and worries about operating it. All three teams have escalated to you, and you have been asked to drive a decision within {{decide_by}}.
sections.problem: How would you drive this to a decision: how you frame it, what evidence you gather, who decides, what options you put forward and how you keep the three teams working together afterwards? Then describe a real technical disagreement you drove to a decision across teams with competing goals (STAR, with the outcome and your own part), or say plainly that you have not and reason through it.
sections.constraints: You do not manage any of the three teams. Any decision must honour existing customer agreements, including customers who have opted out of data retention. The decision must be revisited if it turns out wrong, without a new escalation.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical teams, figures and options. No statement here describes any company's actual logging practice.
sections.criteria: Turns positions into needs and agreed decision criteria; gathers evidence (the debugging cases that failed, what data would have resolved them, the agreements that bind, real cost figures); puts forward several concrete options with trade-offs (for example scoped sampling, redaction, short retention, opt-in or internal traffic, faster access path) and a recommendation; respects privacy's veto and customer agreements; names the decider and a review date with success metrics; keeps relationships intact; real example has evidence, a personal contribution and lessons, or is honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: What regression prompted this?
clarifications.a: A quality drop last month took nine days to diagnose because nobody could see example requests.

clarifications.q: Who has final say?
clarifications.a: A named executive, on your recommendation. Privacy has a veto on anything that breaks an agreement.

clarifications.q: Is there an existing access process for logged data?
clarifications.a: Yes, ticket-based, but research says it takes days.

hints: Reframe positions as needs: what question does research need to answer, what risk does privacy need to avoid, what cost and load can infrastructure carry?
The options are not only "more" or "less": consider scope, sampling, retention, redaction, access path and opt-in sources.
Agree the decision criteria before debating the options.
followups: The research lead says that without full bodies they cannot do their job, and privacy says any bodies at all are unacceptable. How do you move them?
What would you measure in three months to know whether the decision was right?
The executive picks an option you argued against. What do you do next?
In your real example, what did you concede, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: A compromise can leave every team unable to do its job. How do you check the middle option actually solves research's problem?
How do you know the redaction works on free-text prompts, and who signs off that it is good enough?
Is a sample enough to catch a regression that only affects a small slice of traffic?
What do you bring to the executive so the decision is quick and sticks?
